The market's leadership has changed. Many of the mega-ap growth stocks that drove the indexes to new heights in recent years are now lagging.

The Nasdaq-100, which is the 100 largest non-financial stocks in the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC), is up 12.4% year-to-date (YTD) at the time of this writing. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) have produced smaller gains, while Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) are down YTD. This means that six "Magnificent Seven" stocks are underperforming the Nasdaq-100 YTD -- the only exception being Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here's why the Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Growth ETF (NYSEMKT: MGK) is an excellent low-cost way to buy the dip on top growth stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.
The Mega Cap Growth ETF has 67.6% in 10 stocks

The Mega Cap Growth ETF is essentially a more concentrated version of the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (NYSEMKT: VUG). The Mega Cap ETF has 52 holdings compared to 135 for the Growth ETF. The expense ratio of the Mega Cap ETF is 0.05% -- only slightly higher than the Growth ETF's 0.03% expense ratio. It's worth noting that 0.03% is the lowest you'll find for any ETF. The largest ETF by net assets in the world is the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, which also has a 0.03% expense ratio.

AAPL data by YCharts

Because of the sheer size of the largest U.S. companies, the top 10 holdings in the Mega Cap Growth ETF make up a staggering 67.6% of the fund -- including a combined 44.4% in the six "Magnificent Seven" stocks that are underperforming the Nasdaq-100 YTD.

Investing in leading Nasdaq and NYSE growth stocks

The Mega Cap Growth ETF is a great buy for investors who believe today's most valuable companies will continue leading the broader market over the long term. But some investors may lean toward buying a Nasdaq-100 index ETF, such as the popular Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ), rather than the Mega Cap Growth ETF. The issue with that strategy is twofold.

For starters, the Invesco QQQ Trust has a relatively high expense ratio of 0.18%. And, more importantly, it invests exclusively in Nasdaq-listed non-financial companies -- meaning it excludes key growth stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

With the 2026 election in the books, early signs Wednesday point to a positive day for investors, with the three major market indexes pushing higher. The price-weighted Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 3% (as of this writing), the broad-based S&P 500 has gained 1.7%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite is up 1.7%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Helping lead the major indexes higher are the "Big Three" cloud providers, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG), gaining 7.1%, 7%, and 4.1%, respectively, as I write this.

Given the expected shift in the regulatory environment, it might seem counterintuitive that these tech titans would gain ground, but dig a little deeper, and it's easy to see why shareholders are optimistic.

Image source: Getty Images.

Democrats win control of Congress

Democrats have won control of both the House and Senate, and some won high-profile gubernatorial races. Many market watchers expect the Blue Wave to lead to tighter controls and stricter regulations for data centers. The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked a data center boom, with spending projected to reach as much as $5.2 trillion by 2030, according to global management consulting firm McKinsey & Company.

That build-out could come to a screeching halt in the wake of the Blue Wave. Many Democrats campaigned on platforms seeking moratoriums on data center construction. Texas, Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona are the top locations for data center capacity coming online in 2028, with Texas accounting for 41% of new construction. Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas supports a moratorium until the legislature can assess the impact on power, water, and other local resources.

It wasn't just Democrats. There were an estimated 50 data center-related ballot measures across 10 states, with many seeking to ban new construction or enact strict controls. Many are expected to pass once the final ballot count is complete.

Given the prevailing headwinds, why are the hyperscalers rising today? Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet dominate the data center space, accounting for more than half the top 15 data centers by capacity in North America, according to analysis conducted by Axios. Any move to limit new data center construction would increase their dominance by limiting new competition.

title: The Ultimate Dividend Growth Stock to Buy With $2,000 Right Now

Will Healy, The Motley Fool

It's common knowledge that dividend stocks tend to attract more conservative investors. While these stocks rarely experience rapid growth, they tend to be well-suited for wealth preservation and income generation.

Fortunately, many of these stocks also increase their payouts periodically, bolstering their value as long-term holdings. If one is looking to start building a position by investing $2,000 in such a stock, Home Depot (NYSE: HD) is likely an excellent option, and here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Home Depot as a dividend stock

Income investors will like that Home Depot has hiked its dividend for 17 straight years. The retail stock suspended increases in the late 2000s amid the housing crisis. Still, annual payout hikes had also been the norm since Home Depot's first dividend payment in 1987.

At approximately $330 per share, about $1,980 will buy an investor six shares of Home Depot.

Currently, Home Depot shareholders earn $9.32 per share annually in dividends, totaling $55.92 in yearly dividend income for six shares. This amounts to a dividend yield of 2.8%, far above the S&P 500's (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) average of 1.1%.

Investors can likely expect the payout hikes to continue. Over the trailing 12 months, Home Depot generated just over $15.1 billion in free cash flow, well above the $9.3 billion the payout cost the company over the same period. That leaves ample room for rising payouts and investments in the company.

The focus on wealth preservation

As mentioned, today's Home Depot stock is best-suited for investors focused on rising dividend income and wealth preservation. With a footprint of more than 2,360 stores, the company now adds few new locations annually. The U.S. and Canadian markets offer little opportunity for new development, and past efforts at international expansion failed, effectively limiting growth.

Nonetheless, Home Depot has responded to that challenge by leaning into strategies such as targeting professional contractors in addition to its traditional do-it-yourself customer base. Omnichannel retail, private label brands, and value-added services and rentals have also boosted revenues.

Amid that approach, it reported $89 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, a 5% yearly increase. Net income rose by under 1% to almost $8.1 billion over the same period due to higher operating costs.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) has been one of the top-performing stocks in 2026, clocking impressive gains of over 120% as of this writing, and the good news is that it can deliver further gains to investors thanks to an acceleration in growth.

AMD released its third-quarter results on Nov. 3, and the stock soared the following day. Let's see why that was the case and check how much upside this fast-growing semiconductor stock could deliver by the end of the decade.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: AMD.
AMD's data center business has supercharged its growth

AMD's Q3 revenue increased 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. The company's non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.09 increased by 74% from the year-ago period. AMD's data center business was the primary driver of its impressive growth, with the segment's revenue nearly doubling year over year to a record $8.5 billion.

It is worth noting that AMD's revenue and earnings easily exceeded Wall Street's expectations. The company noted healthy demand for its Epyc server processors and Instinct data center graphics cards. The good news for AMD investors is that the company expects data center revenue to accelerate in the current quarter. What's more, its full-year data center revenue is on track to double from 2025 levels.

Looking ahead, AMD expects the data center segment to account for 80% of its top line in 2027. That implies a major improvement over the previous quarter, when the data center segment produced 64% of AMD's top line. Moreover, the increasing reliance on the data center business is a good sign for AMD, given the ongoing weakness in the personal computer market.

AMD reported an 8% year-over-year decline in its client and gaming segment revenue last quarter to $3.7 billion. Notably, its PC-focused client processor revenue increased 7% from the year-ago period despite a 21% decline in PC industry shipments last quarter. The gaming segment continues to struggle due to the aging gaming console generation. However, the potential arrival of a new generation of gaming consoles next year could lift this segment and complement the healthy growth AMD has been witnessing in data centers.

Importantly, AMD expects significant acceleration in growth despite challenging conditions in the gaming and PC markets. The company expects revenue to increase by 66% year over year in the current quarter, a substantial step up from the 45% growth seen in the previous one.

Schneider Electric has recently ramped up its AI focused data center offering, introducing its RapidScale Modular Data Center Reference Design 115, new liquid cooling and power gear, and a collaboration with NVIDIA and HPE to support high density AI workloads at the edge and in large facilities.

The push into prefabricated AI infrastructure and edge Physical AI solutions points to Schneider Electric targeting faster deployment cycles, tighter control of equipment supply, and deeper integration of software and hardware across data center and industrial customers.

Next, the focus will be on how this AI centric data center build out could shape Schneider Electric's broader investment narrative.

Spot potential second movers around Schneider Electric's AI build out by scanning our hand picked 53 AI infrastructure stocks, which is shaping the next wave of high density data centers and power systems.

Schneider Electric Investment Narrative Recap

To own Schneider Electric, you need to believe in a long runway for electrification, AI-heavy infrastructure and higher margin software, all while the group manages a more leveraged balance sheet. The €6,000m senior bond issue at an average 4.3% coupon leans into that belief, since it funds the all-cash PTC deal on top of a recent €6,000m equity raise.

The short-term swing factor is execution on PTC integration and Industrial Automation margins without letting interest costs and higher debt crowd out flexibility. The bond terms spread maturities out to 2046, which helps liquidity planning, but leverage and integration risk remain the clearest near-term overhang for Schneider Electric.

The PTC-funded bond issue sits alongside Schneider Electric's wider push into AI-ready infrastructure, where the RapidScale Modular Data Center blueprint and Physical AI work with NVIDIA and HPE aim to turn AI demand into repeatable projects. Those contracts matter because they could support Energy Management and Industrial Automation activity if orders translate into real deployments.

For shareholders, the link is simple. If Schneider Electric can convert this AI-centric pipeline into steady, higher value projects while absorbing PTC cleanly, the added software and services exposure may help offset the higher interest burden. Any stumble on execution, cost discipline or integration would make that larger capital structure feel heavier very quickly.

Schneider Electric's analyst narrative points to forecast revenues of €58.1 billion and earnings of €8.7 billion by 2029, based on 11.4% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about €4.0 billion from €4.7 billion today.

CrowdStrike recently announced an integrated Falcon security offering for the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA. At the same time, Dell expanded its own AI-focused cybersecurity, data protection and AI infrastructure services, including quantum-safe encryption, identity resilience tools and managed detection and response across AI workloads.

These moves deepen Dell Technologies' role in securing enterprise AI stacks end to end, from data center infrastructure and AI servers to identity systems and managed security operations. This is directly tied to a large AI server order backlog that anchors demand for its broader infrastructure and services portfolio.

The focus now shifts to what this broader AI security and infrastructure push means for Dell Technologies' existing investment narrative, which has been built around large AI server backlogs.

Scan beyond Dell Technologies' AI security push and line up other potential beneficiaries of the same trend with our curated list of 53 AI infrastructure stocks.

Dell Technologies Investment Narrative Recap

For an investor in Dell Technologies, the core belief is that its US$95b AI server backlog and wider AI infrastructure portfolio can keep filling factories and data centers while higher margin storage and services scale alongside. The near term swing factor is how efficiently that backlog converts into shipped systems and cash without eroding profitability.

The biggest risk right now is that tight supply across memory, CPUs and other components, together with weaker PC demand and pricing pressure in traditional hardware, puts a ceiling on margin progress. The latest AI security announcements look additive to the thesis but do not materially change that near term catalyst and risk equation yet.

The CrowdStrike Falcon integration into the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA looks most relevant here because it ties security directly to the same AI server footprint that underpins Dell Technologies' backlog. Customers can procure infrastructure and Falcon protection together, with Dell Managed Detection and Response wrapped around those workloads.

That matters for the thesis because security and resilience can influence which vendor wins enterprise AI standardization, which in turn affects how much of the US$130b AI order flow sticks with Dell. Execution risk sits in scaling these services profitably, since AI servers currently carry mid single digit operating margins and mix shift remains a key watchpoint.

Dell Technologies' current analyst storyline points to US$266.7b in revenue and US$20.8b in earnings by 2029, which implies 20.8% yearly top line growth and an earnings increase of about US$9.4b from US$11.4b today.

Uber reported its third quarter results this morning as markets rallied.

Gross bookings rose 20% to $59.8 billion, trips increased 16% to 4.1 billion, and revenue grew 10% to $14.8 billion. The stock closed up about 5%.

The biggest "miss," if we can call it that, was GAAP diluted EPS: 25 cents, compared with the 96 cents expected by analysts polled by LSEG. Adjusted EPS of 88 cents, however, topped most estimates. The gap was largely due to a $476 million net pre-tax loss from revaluing Uber's equity stakes.

Revenue in Uber's core mobility unit, its ride-hailing service, also declined 2% to $7.52 billion, even as mobility bookings grew 18%. That fell short of StreetAccount's $7.71 billion estimate, CNBC reported.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

"Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in prepared remarks. He added that Uber is making "targeted investments to strengthen driver supply."

Freight, Uber's logistics unit, which matches businesses' shipments with trucking carriers, drove the overall revenue beat. Sales rose 34% to $1.76 billion, topping StreetAccount's $1.49 billion estimate. Food delivery revenue also climbed 23% to $5.49 billion, just shy of the $5.51 billion average estimate.

Rather than making money moving people, Uber is finding growth in shipping goods and delivering food. Waymo wasn't mentioned, which is notable given the gradual separation underway between the two companies. In July, Uber said Waymo had told it that the Waymo app is set to launch in Austin and Atlanta in January 2028, alongside its existing Uber deployment. That's still a ways off, but given Waymo's popularity, Uber appears to be diversifying its revenue in preparation.
